newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian wheat imports seen dipping as prices ease.
newsitem.headline: Indian wheat imports seen dipping as prices ease.

text.p: A dip in domestic wheat prices and hopes of a good crop might prompt India to buy less than the two million tonnes of wheat it planned to import by March, traders and analysts said on Friday.

"I don't think they (government) will buy two million tonnes. The world market prices have gone up and domestic wheat as on date is cheaper," Pradeep Kotak, a leading Bombay foodgrains exporter, told Reuters.
The government-run State Trading Corporation (STC) has so far contracted to import 1.25 million tonnes of wheat in 1996/97 (April-March), officials said.
The corporation on Tuesday tendered to import another 50,000 tonnes of wheat for arrivals by the end of March.
In December, India decided to import two million tonnes of wheat in the current financial year to augment domestic supplies and check rising prices.

India last imported wheat in 1992/93, buying two million tonnes of wheat. It exported 600,000 tonnes in 1995/96 and 1.07 million tonnes between April and September 1996, when the government halted exports.
STC officials said India was focusing on Argentina, Australia and Canada as suppliers.

"Because of the government decision hoarders have released their stocks," Kotak said. "Wheat prices have come down by 500-1,000 rupees per tonne in different pockets depending on the quality and state due to a psychological reaction."
"Already the impact is being felt in the market and once one or two ships (with imported wheat) arrive, it will have a salutary effect," said one analyst.
Traders said wheat prices in the domestic markets were ruling on an average of 6,200 rupees ($174) per tonne, compared with a high of 7,700 rupees in October-November.

An official of the state-owned Food Corporation of India, which will handle the imported wheat, said one shipload had already arrived in the southern port of Vishakhapatnam and another was due at Nhava Sheva port near Bombay on Sunday.
Chicago Board of Trade (CBOT) wheat futures closed lower on Thursday on diminishing hopes that India would be buying large amounts of wheat from the world market.
"We foresee that the imports will not come. It is not required. There is enough wheat in the country," said O.P. Mangal of Space Group, a Delhi foodgrains exporter.
Analysts said India was expecting a good summer wheat crop due for harvest in March after a ninth consecutive good monsoon.
India expects a wheat crop of about 64 milion tonnes in 1996/97 (October-September) against 62.3 million in 1995/96. A clear picture should emerge by early February.
Government wheat procurement in the 1995/96 growing season fell to 8.2 million tonnes from 12.3 million tonnes in the previous year due to a three-million-tonne shortfall in output.
Officials said as of January 1, the government had wheat stocks of 6.7 million tonnes, about one million tonnes less than the buffer stock requirement on that date.

Food Minister Devendra Prasad Yadav said on Tuesday that in view of the depleted wheat stocks the government might have to examine various options including bringing forward the procurement season by a fortnight to March 16.
"I think they will buy all the two million tonnes but shipments may get delayed. It is impossible for all the volume to come (by March)," said Deepak Tanna, another trader. ($1 = 35.80 rupees)
